title: Who Should Hold the Purse Strings? Mayors on Fiscal Devolution
label: 15 September 2026 · Fiscal devolution
summary: The Economic Affairs Committee heard from Howard Dawber, Deputy Mayor of London, and Lord Houchen, Metro Mayor of Tees Valley, about the Government's plans for fiscal devolution in England. Both mayors broadly welcomed the move towards greater local control over funding, but Lord Houchen argued it is not true fiscal devolution, merely a block grant replacing separate grants. The discussion covered the need for equalisation between richer and poorer areas, the potential to borrow against devolved taxes, the risk of widening regional gaps, and the tension between regional mayors and local councils.

speakers.label: Howard Dawber
speakers.name: Howard Dawber OBE
speakers.role: Deputy Mayor for Business and Growth, London City Hall

chapters.title: What the mayors want
chapters.takeaway: Both witnesses broadly welcome devolution but disagree on whether the Government's plans are real fiscal devolution.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Welcome. Let's start with a simple question: will fiscal devolution boost economic growth in your areas?

turns.speaker: Howard Dawber
turns.text: Yes, I think it will. Take Crossrail, the Elizabeth line. We spent years campaigning for it, and it could have been done much faster if the Mayor of London had more control over the funding. We had to get legislation and work with governments to create things like a business rate supplement and a mayoral levy to pay for it. With income tax devolution, mayors could borrow against it, unlike the grants we get now. That would make a real difference.

turns.speaker: Lord Houchen of High Leven
turns.text: I come at this differently. What's being proposed isn't actually fiscal devolution. It's replacing a bunch of grants with a single block grant - a Section 31 grant - and calling it 'equivalent to 3% of income tax'. But they're not giving us income tax, just a fixed pot with fewer strings. It's more about flexibility and long-term certainty than real tax-raising power. If it's just like-for-like, it doesn't give us much extra. If it's additional, that's different - it lets us plan and invest and borrow.

chapters.title: Borrowing and accountability
chapters.takeaway: Devolving income tax could let mayors borrow for infrastructure, but the certainty of that income compared to grants is debated.

turns.speaker: Lord Young of Cookham
turns.text: Howard, you said the key difference is being able to borrow against future income tax. But local authorities can already borrow prudentially. Are you really saying that income tax is more secure than grants?

turns.speaker: Howard Dawber
turns.text: In practice, yes. We can't borrow against grants because a future government could just cut them. Income tax is more reliable, and financial institutions would treat it differently. We've borrowed against future farebox for Crossrail, and we'd like to do similar deals for things like the DLR extension. More fiscal autonomy means more ability to invest.

turns.speaker: Lord Houchen of High Leven
turns.text: I'd say yes, it would help. But combined authorities have a hard borrowing cap, unlike local authorities. Even with a good business case, we can't borrow beyond a limit. The Treasury is looking at caps and collars on income tax to manage fluctuations. And remember, some projects like bus franchising can't be financed commercially anyway - they need subsidy. The market will only lend against a guaranteed income stream, which often means the government covenant.

chapters.title: Which taxes to devolve?
chapters.takeaway: Income tax and business rates are the most suitable taxes for devolution because they are stable, locally identifiable, and linked to growth.

turns.speaker: Lord Petitgas
turns.text: In an ideal world, which taxes should be devolved or assigned to local areas?

turns.speaker: Howard Dawber
turns.text: There are four tests: does it grow with the local economy, is it stable enough to borrow against, can you point to where it's raised and spent, and can the public see the link between tax and decision? Income tax and business rates fit well. VAT is hard because of online sales. A visitor levy works because it's local. We're at the start of a journey.

turns.speaker: Lord Houchen of High Leven
turns.text: I agree. Business rate retention is already working in Teesside - we keep rates from the SeAH wind factory, which will generate billions over 15-20 years. But we must avoid the trap local authorities fell into: when the rate base declines, they lose interest in attracting investment because equalisation means they won't gain. We need a floor. And income tax equalisation is vital - without it, London would get £2.3bn while Teesside gets £170m, baking in left-behind areas. But too much equalisation can create inertia.

chapters.title: Equalisation dilemma
chapters.takeaway: The witnesses disagree on whether equalisation should start from the status quo or involve a transfer from London to poorer areas on day one.

turns.speaker: Lord Prentis of Leeds
turns.text: How worried should we be about underperformance if devolution rewards success? What form should equalisation take?

turns.speaker: Howard Dawber
turns.text: This isn't a zero-sum game. Our principle: start in neutral so no area is worse off, then let places keep a meaningful share of growth for long enough to make a difference. If you equalise every penny away, you've just reinvented the grant. Equalise the starting point, not the growth. Lock it in for about 10 years. And protect areas from national decisions they don't control, like a national income tax cut.

turns.speaker: Lord Houchen of High Leven
turns.text: The regulation here is crucial. You can't allow areas to fail and lose income without a backstop - government will always step in. So what's the point? You need to reduce the downside without removing the incentive to grow. But you also risk areas saying, 'We'll just wait for a top-up.' London has been supportive of equalisation, but if it's a pure free-for-all, Teesside and places like it will never catch up. The macro economy always drowns out local efforts.

turns.speaker: Lord Newby
turns.text: Ben, you said decades of underinvestment. So you'd want a different starting point than Howard's neutral one?

turns.speaker: Lord Houchen of High Leven
turns.text: It depends on what you mean by neutral. If it means equalising London and Teesside pound for pound, I'd take that. But the reality is that without a transfer from London on day one, the disparity is too great. Otherwise, we get £170m and London gets £2.3bn, and we keep the upside? That will never equalise. There will be a political bunfight.

turns.speaker: Howard Dawber
turns.text: That's why we say start from where we are now and incentivise growth. If London kept all its income tax, that would be a massive change. We're happy for the fiscal transfer to go up, but it must be 'and', not 'instead of'. London's growth helps the whole country.

chapters.title: Devolution to mayors vs councils
chapters.takeaway: Devolution is going primarily to regional mayors, not local councils, raising questions about democratic accountability and the future of local government.

turns.speaker: Lord Carrington of Fulham
turns.text: How much devolution should go to local authorities as opposed to strategic authorities?

turns.speaker: Howard Dawber
turns.text: London is different - we have a directly elected mayor and assembly. Local authorities have very little room for manoeuvre now because of social care and temporary accommodation costs. There's a case for reviewing local government funding in parallel, but we work closely with London Councils. For now, the devolution on the table is mainly from national to regional government.

turns.speaker: Lord Houchen of High Leven
turns.text: The clear direction is prioritising regional mayors over local authorities. For example, the Prime Minister gave homelessness funding to regional authorities, not councils. In practice, we pass it through to councils because they deliver it. But the policy is regional. On democratic accountability: most people can't name their local councillor. Mayors have higher turnout and clearer accountability. But we still have to work closely with councils, and there will be tensions.

turns.speaker: Lord Carrington of Fulham
turns.text: Aren't we moving towards regional government with mayors dictating to local councils? And housing, for instance, is archetypally local.

turns.speaker: Howard Dawber
turns.text: In London we have strategic planning and housing powers, but detailed decisions are for local authorities. We only intervene in a minority of large schemes. The key is being clear about who does what. We don't want mayors to be a surrogate Whitehall controlling local government.

chapters.title: Boundaries, planning and conflict
chapters.takeaway: Blurred boundaries between councils and mayors will cause friction, especially over planning, but London shows a model of close collaboration.

turns.speaker: Baroness Wheatcroft
turns.text: Will blurred boundaries between local and strategic authorities cause constant conflict?

turns.speaker: Lord Houchen of High Leven
turns.text: Yes, there will be tension. The Government might be tempted to give more powers to regions as councils struggle. We need to guard against powers moving up from local communities. And planning will be a flashpoint - I intend to use call-in powers to drive growth, which will disgruntle some local councillors.

turns.speaker: Howard Dawber
turns.text: In London we have separate but collaborative structures. We developed an economic growth plan jointly with all the boroughs. Collaboration is built in, not structurally required. There will be political disagreements, but that's democracy. I'm not worried about conflict, because we work together.

turns.speaker: Baroness Wheatcroft
turns.text: Andy Burnham said mayors will get powers to override local authorities on planning. Is that dangerous?

turns.speaker: Lord Houchen of High Leven
turns.text: I slightly fear it. Devolution started collegiately, but now more powers are vested solely in mayors. We'll see friction, but I'm happy to make tough decisions and be held accountable at the ballot box.

chapters.title: Checks, balances and capability
chapters.takeaway: Mayoral decisions need robust audit trails, and there are big capability differences between regional authorities and local councils.

turns.speaker: Lord Burns
turns.text: Ben, do you take planning decisions alone? What checks are there?

turns.speaker: Lord Houchen of High Leven
turns.text: I still have to act within the law and have valid planning reasons. Decisions can be appealed or judicially reviewed. There will be audit trails to ensure robustness. But standards may vary between mayors, so government might want to equalise.

turns.speaker: Lord Razzall
turns.text: Is democratic accountability clear between mayors and strategic authorities? And what about areas without mayors?

turns.speaker: Howard Dawber
turns.text: In London we have the Assembly to scrutinise the mayor, plus the four-year electoral cycle. The buck stops with the mayor. It's clear who took a decision. In areas without a mayor, if Government prioritises mayors, they will lose out. But offering the positive advantages of a mayoral model is better than imposing it.

turns.speaker: Lord Houchen of High Leven
turns.text: I agree. If you want devolution everywhere, you might have to impose it, because politics gets in the way. Some areas fear a mayor from a different party. But without a mayor, you're at a disadvantage. The Government seems to accept different tiers, which is unhelpful for accountability.

chapters.title: Reorganisation and skills gaps
chapters.takeaway: Local government reorganisation should not hold back devolution, but there are real differences in capacity between regions and councils.

turns.speaker: Baroness Alexander of Cleveden
turns.text: What are the implications of the Government pausing local government reorganisation?

turns.speaker: Howard Dawber
turns.text: The pause shouldn't hold back devolution to existing mayoral structures. Reorganisation and devolution are separate. We shouldn't wait for a perfect system everywhere. Businesses find multiple tiers confusing, but that's no reason to delay.

turns.speaker: Lord Houchen of High Leven
turns.text: I agree. If you want more devolution, allow areas to come together in existing models. Whitehall has long wanted unitary councils, but that policy is now unclear. We should avoid raising powers up from local councils while waiting.

turns.speaker: Lord Reid of Cardowan
turns.text: Do you worry about inequality in skills and capacity between regional authorities and local councils? Will local councils lose out?

turns.speaker: Lord Houchen of High Leven
turns.text: Yes, there will be disparities. We have 160 staff; South Yorkshire has 450-500. London is years ahead. Capability varies. But we collaborate and help each other. Our competition is international, not each other.

turns.speaker: Howard Dawber
turns.text: There is a disparity. London's mayoral operation is larger than some government departments. We have a responsibility to help other mayors build capability. Collaboration across regions and parties is one of the most exciting parts of devolution. We're not in competition with Teesside - we're competing with New York, Dubai, Singapore.
